fields.v: Lekarakos, A. I., Koutsomitropoulos, D. A., Tsolis, D. K. (2026). Towards an Evaluation Methodology for AI Code Assistants. In: 2026 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA), pp. 1-8. IEEE. https://doi.org/10.1109/IISA71656.2026.11705481
Conference — 2026 17th International Conference on Information, Intelligence, Systems & Applications (IISA), IEEE, pp. 1-8, DOI 10.1109/IISA71656.2026.11705481
Computer Engineering and Informatics Department, University of Patras, Greece (all authors; academic)

Proposes an evaluation method; secondary: Compares — AI-DevEval framework (four axes: Efficiency & Flow, Feature Richness, Context Engineering, User Experience; weighted AI-Dev Index with quality zones) applied in an exploratory controlled study with 6 developers comparing a web chatbot, an IDE plugin and an AI-native IDE, plus a model-volatility comparison

No SDD approach. Tools compared: Claude Web (chatbot baseline, Chrome), GitHub Copilot (VS Code plugin), Google Antigravity (AI-native IDE); model fixed to Claude Sonnet 4.6 in the primary phase; secondary phase Antigravity with Gemini 3 Flash vs Claude Sonnet 4.6; tool versions not stated
N/A (no specification artefacts; Context Engineering axis scores configuration-as-code rule files such as .cursorrules/.windsurfrules, .aiignore, global rules and memory features)
N/A (interactive use of assistants by developers; no prescribed flow)
Developer reviews and corrects AI suggestions throughout (measured as review ratio Rrev); no prescribed review points
N/A (no SDD approach; full interactive use of each assistant on three tasks)
Not classifiable (no SDD; authors' wording 'context engineering', 'orchestration layer')

Existing code base: MVP-stage 'Delivery on Demand' food delivery application; three scenarios: greenfield Admin dashboard feature, multi-file i18n refactoring of Courier views, full-stack admin customer endpoint with an intentional password-leak vulnerability

One application (React/Next.js frontend, Node.js backend, PostgreSQL with Prisma); 3 scenarios; size of the code base Not stated; 6 participants, each solving the 3 scenarios with a different tool (Latin square)
Web development (food delivery application with Admin and Courier roles)

6 individual participants: 2 senior undergraduate CS students, 2 mid-level engineers (2-5 years), 2 senior engineers (> 5 years); demographic profile (experience, usage context, AI familiarity) collected
Completion time Tc (minutes, prompt submission to successful execution); number of prompts Np (values not reported); no token or money cost
None (no tests; 'successful execution' ends Tc but its criterion is not defined); detection of the intentional data leak used qualitatively in scenario 3
None

Interaction friction If (copy-paste + window switches + file adds); review ratio Rrev (review/correction time over generation time, target < 1); number of prompts; 10-item DX-Q questionnaire on 5-point Likert (learning, flow, trust; includes cognitive load); overall subjective score 0-10

Feature Richness score (7 features, 0-3 each, max 21); Context Engineering Score (4 dimensions, 0-3 each, max 12); AI-Dev Index Itotal = 0.35 Ictx + 0.30 Ieff + 0.20 Idx + 0.15 Ifeat with min-max normalisation (0-100) and quality zones (< 40, 40-65, 65-85, >= 85); model volatility

Manual: post-session analysis of screen and audio recordings (Tc, Np, If, Rrev); think-aloud and observational notes; questionnaire after each scenario; feature and context scores by rubric (scorer not stated). Min-max normalisation across the tools evaluated

Exploratory study, 6 participants (Table V, VII). Authors' criterion: AI-Dev Index quality zones (Zone 1 Insufficient < 40 ... Zone 4 Autonomous Agent >= 85); Rrev target < 1. Claude Web + Claude Sonnet 4.6 (baseline): A1 0.01, A2 23.8, A3 25.0, A4 60.0, Itotal 24.32 (Zone 1); Tc 42.8 min, If 80.1, Rrev 0.87 — quality verdict: does not work (Zone 1); cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. GitHub Copilot (VS Code) + Claude Sonnet 4.6: A1 70.87, A2 71.4, A3 75.0, A4 72.0, Itotal 72.62 (Zone 3); Tc 22.3 min, If 7.2, Rrev 0.42 — quality verdict: partly (Zone 3, requires supervision); cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. Google Antigravity + Claude Sonnet 4.6: A1 100.0, A2 95.2, A3 100.0, A4 96.0, Itotal 98.48 (Zone 4); Tc 10.6 min, If 4.5, Rrev 0.15; overall subjective 9.8/10 — quality verdict: works (Zone 4); cost verdict: no criterion stated by the authors. Secondary phase (Table VIII): Antigravity + Gemini 3 Flash: A1 87.84, Itotal 94.83 (Zone 4), Tc 8.5 min, more prompts and higher Rrev — quality verdict: works (Zone 4); Antigravity + Claude Sonnet 4.6: A1 98.47, Itotal 98.02, Tc 10.6 min — works (Zone 4); cost verdicts: no criterion stated by the authors
fields.why: Metric values check out against Tables V, VII and VIII (Table VIII columns confirmed by recomputing Itotal with Eq. 2). The quality zones are the authors' own classification, but they rate integration/DX on a min-max index relative to the three tools (the chatbot is near 0 by construction), not the quality of the code produced, so reading Zone 1/3/4 as does not work/partly/works is the extractor's mapping. Also, Table I sets a stated target Rrev < 1, met by all three tools (0.87, 0.42, 0.15), which could support an effort/cost verdict that the draft does not use
fields.doubt: As zonas do AI-Dev Index medem integração/DX relativa às três ferramentas, não a qualidade do código; a meta Rrev < 1 é cumprida por todas. Decide se servem de critério ou se fica 'no criterion stated by the authors'.

fields.v: One project, 3 scenarios of escalating complexity; 3 tools with the model fixed to Claude Sonnet 4.6 (to isolate the tool's contribution); baseline Claude Web; 6 participants of three seniority levels in a counterbalanced Latin-square design (each participant uses each tool once, on a different scenario); secondary phase swaps the model (Gemini 3 Flash vs Claude Sonnet 4.6) in Antigravity, participants not stated. No acceptance tests. One session per participant-scenario. Human intervention: humans operate the tools interactively; sessions recorded

Antigravity > Copilot > Claude Web on every axis (Itotal 98.48 / 72.62 / 24.32); Tc 10.6 / 22.3 / 42.8 min (SD ±1.5 / ±3.2 / ±6.4), If 4.5 / 7.2 / 80.1, Rrev 0.15 / 0.42 / 0.87; ordering preserved for every participant and under four weighting schemes (Table VI). Model swap changed only A1 (Gemini faster but more prompts and higher Rrev; index 94.83 vs 98.02, both Zone 4). Index aligned with subjective satisfaction (> 90%, Fig. 3). No statistical significance tests

Distinguished the three tools consistently (per participant and across weightings); repeatability not assessed beyond per-participant ordering. Limitations: N = 6 exploratory; seniority effects only qualitative; single full-stack web project; task-complexity bias (simpler tasks may narrow gaps). Not stated by the authors: min-max normalisation makes the index relative to the tools compared, and the 'validation' uses the same participants' overall score

Limitations: small sample (N = 6) in an exploratory mixed-methods design; single web project; task-complexity bias; seniority not stratified quantitatively. Future work: projects of greater architectural depth; automated metric extraction through IDE telemetry; measuring degree of autonomy of multi-agent systems; Code Retained metric; longitudinal studies; seniority gap and 'AI-Auditing' pedagogy

No replication package or materials; no pre-registration. Languages: JavaScript/TypeScript (React/Next.js, Node.js) with Prisma/PostgreSQL. Inconsistencies: Antigravity + Claude Sonnet 4.6 scores A1 100.0 / Itotal 98.48 in Table V but A1 98.47 / Itotal 98.02 in Table VIII; Table V gives Claude A1 = 0.01 while its footnote says 0.0; Np defined but never reported; abstract says tools 'significantly reduce' friction without any statistical test; how 'successful execution' was judged is not stated; '> 90% alignment' (Fig. 3) not defined; per-tool averages mix different scenarios because of the Latin square.
